description: Turning raw data into insight. Interests: data analytics, ML for scientific data, remote sensing and astronomy.
summary: I developed a web application that turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent burning-activity calendar for any area of Ukraine. MODIS and VIIRS records cannot be compared directly: VIIRS detects about three times more hot spots, so merged records show a false jump in 2012. The app harmonizes MODIS to the VIIRS scale with a model chosen by leave-one-year-out validation (9.7% monthly error, against 16.2% for a single ratio), and continues the record with NOAA-20 after S-NPP ended. Users select an area and dates to see critical weeks, anomalies, the current month against the historical median, and season trends, and can download hot spots as CSV. Beyond the challenge, fire events are classified as crop-residue, grass, forest or peat burning (78% agreement in a manual check), and burning upwind of Kyiv is traced. This matters: fire managers need a consistent record to plan monitoring and response, and Kyiv suffers recurring smoke. The analysis shows that spring burning now starts about 9 days per decade earlier, and that crop-residue burning in Kyiv, Cherkasy and Zhytomyr oblasts dominates upwind fire load on poor-air days.
details:
What it does.

My web app turns 26 years of satellite active-fire detections into one consistent burning-activity calendar for any area of Ukraine. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) see fires very differently: VIIRS records 5–6× more hot spots because it resolves small fires. As a result, merged records show a false “jump” in 2012. I harmonize MODIS to the VIIRS S-NPP scale and continue the record with NOAA-20 after S-NPP data delivery ended in November 2026. The result is shown as:

  • calendar heatmaps by week × year and month × year, with 80/95% uncertainty intervals;
  • a “this month vs historical median” panel;
  • percentile anomalies;
  • critical weeks;
  • season onset, peak and end, plus long-term trends;
  • CSV downloads of the calendar and the individual hot spots, and PNG export of every chart.

Users choose an area as a preset, a point plus radius, or a drawn polygon.

How it works.

  • Data preparation: NASA FIRMS archive and near-real-time data (MODIS C6.1; VIIRS S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21), filtered to vegetation fires.
  • Harmonization: four models compared with leave-one-year-out validation. The winner, a VIIRS/MODIS ratio by month and day/night, has 9.7% monthly error for Ukraine, against 16.2% for a single ratio. A more complex GLM did not do better.
  • Uncertainty: intervals are calibrated on held-out errors; the cross-validated coverage of 80% intervals is 72–81%.
  • Burn-type classification: VIIRS detections are clustered into 446,676 fire events in space and time. Transparent rules on land cover (ESA WorldCover, PEATMAP), duration, night fraction and fire radiative power assign each event a type. The rules agree with an unsupervised Gaussian-mixture model for 84% of events, and with a manual NASA Worldview check for 78% (95% CI 55–91%, 18 events).
  • Kyiv air: a daily “upwind fire load” for Kyiv. It sums the fire power of detections within 300 km that lie upwind of the city (ERA5 wind), including fires in Belarus, and compares it with PM2.5 from the CAMS model and OpenAQ ground stations.

Benefits and intended impact.

  • Emergency responders and land managers see when burning is typically high (the critical weeks are late March to mid-April and late July to August) and how the current month compares with history, on one consistent scale across sensors.
  • Scientists get a documented, uncertainty-aware record with all validation numbers.
  • Kyiv authorities get an evidence-based picture of what burns upwind on poor-air days, and where. About 64% of the upwind fire load is crop-residue burning, mainly in Kyiv, Cherkasy and Zhytomyr oblasts. This is presented as an association that can guide where to target burning control.

Tools.

  • Language and libraries: Python 3.13 with pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, scikit-learn, GeoPandas, Shapely, rasterio, Matplotlib and Plotly.
  • App and hosting: Streamlit with Folium, deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud with code on GitHub.
  • AI assistance: Claude Code.

What’s creative about it.

  • It goes beyond harmonization to automatic burn-type classification and a link to a capital city’s air quality, including cross-border fires.
  • It is honest about what is uncertain: every estimate carries an interval, the model was chosen by validation rather than complexity, and the app states openly what is not validated. For example, the CAMS model misses the April 2020 Kyiv smoke episode, when Kyiv was rated the world’s most polluted city.

Factors considered.

  • Scientific rules: a detection is an observation, not a fire, so MODIS and VIIRS counts are never added together. No detection does not mean no fire. Associations are not causation, and the app makes no forecasts.
  • The war: conflict-affected oblasts are flagged at oblast level, without claiming any detection is war-caused. They can be excluded consistently across all years so trends compare like with like.
  • Usability: the app runs fast from small processed files.

Use of AI tools

The code, analysis pipeline, app and documentation were developed with an AI coding assistant (Anthropic Claude, via Claude Code) under the author’s direction. The author defined the research questions, scientific rules and validation requirements, made the key method decisions (e.g. constant-area trends, conflict-zone handling, baseline choice), reviewed all results, and manually labelled the 40 validation events in NASA Worldview. All numbers come from real data processed by the code in the repository; no synthetic data were used. All figures and charts are data plots rendered by our code with Matplotlib and Plotly, and app screenshots were taken with a headless browser.
